items.title: 10.4 Motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field

source_refs.note: Topic 10.4 with Fig. 10.10, Example 10.3 and the side boxes (PDF 234-236, printed 231-233). The text cites Fig. 10.8 for the left-hand rule (Fig. 10.3); recorded.

blocks.text: A current-carrying conductor placed perpendicularly in a uniform magnetic field experiences a force F. Since a current is the flow of electric charges, this raises the question: do individual charges moving through a magnetic field also experience a force? The answer is yes; experiments show that a charged particle does experience a force when it moves across a magnetic field. We can calculate this force by examining the behaviour of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

Consider a conductor of length L through which N charged particles, each with charge q, are passing in time t. The motion of these particles produces a current I = Q/t = Nq/t, where Q is the total charge flowing in time t. If v is the velocity of the charged particles, their velocity along the conductor is v = v L(hat), where L(hat) is the unit vector in the direction of the current. The sign of the force depends on whether q is positive or negative; L(hat) is directed along the current, which is the direction of motion of positive charges. Since the particles take time t to cross the conductor of length L, t = L/v, so I = Nq/t = Nqv/L ... (10.8).

If this conductor is placed in a uniform magnetic field B, it experiences the force F = I L x B ... (10.9). As L = L L(hat) ... (10.10), substituting I and L gives F = (Nqv/L)(L L(hat) x B), or F = Nqv L(hat) x B ... (10.11). As the velocity v is directed along the conductor, F = Nq v x B ... (10.12). Therefore the force on a single particle is F = q v x B ... (10.13).

blocks.title: Magnetic force on a moving charge
blocks.text: F = q v x B (10.13). If theta is the angle between B and v, the magnitude is F = qvB sin theta ... (10.14). The force is maximum when B is perpendicular to v (theta = 90 degrees) and zero when B is along v (theta = 0).
The direction of force can be known by applying Fleming's left-hand rule or the right-hand rule as shown in Fig. (10.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book cites Fig. (10.8) for Fleming's left-hand rule, but Fig. 10.8 is the loop in a magnetic field of Example 10.2. Fleming's left-hand rule is shown in Fig. 10.3.

items: A positively charged particle entering the field (B into the paper) along the dotted line experiences an upward force and is deflected along a curved path (Fig. 10.10a).
A negatively charged particle is deflected downward by the force acting on it (Fig. 10.10b).

blocks.alt: Two panels with blue crosses for B into the paper. (a) A positive charge +q enters from the left along a dashed straight line with velocity v; a force F points up and its path curves upward. (b) A negative charge -q enters the same way; the force F points down and its path curves downward.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.10: (a) A positive and (b) a negative charge entering a magnetic field directed into the paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.10).

blocks.title: Example 10.3
blocks.text: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with a speed of 10^4 m s^-1. What path will it follow inside the field? (B = 2.5 Wb m^-2, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.) Solution: F = qvB sin theta; as v is perpendicular to B, theta = 90 degrees and q = e, so F = evB. Since F acts perpendicular to v, it provides the centripetal force that keeps the electron in a circle of radius r: evB = mv^2/r, so r = mv/(eB) = (9.11 x 10^-31 kg x 10^4 m s^-1)/(1.6 x 10^-19 C x 2.5 Wb m^-2) = 2.3 x 10^-8 m. The path is a circle of radius 2.3 x 10^-8 m.

Like electric field lines, magnetic field lines never cross each other, but instead push apart from each other (Do You Know). Why does the picture on a television screen, computer monitor or oscilloscope become distorted when a bar magnet is brought near it? (Point to ponder).
